extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and peer-reviewers (especially in biology and medicine) interested in peer-review reform and post-publication review models
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and principles for operating and evaluating post-publication peer-review systems (both primary open refereeing and secondary expert recommendation) in the life sciences; aimed at implementers, reviewers, and readers. Focuses on what to assess in submitted papers, how to run review workflows, and how to communicate status transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary assessment — 'good science' (validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important task for our referees is to tell us immediately whether or not an article is good science ... we simply want to know that it’s valid; that it’s sensible work, carefully done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees should focus on scientific validity rather than whether the work is exciting or novel. The vast majority of submissions are expected to be approved as 'good science.' If an article is not good science, or if a referee has reservations, the referee must add a report describing the problems and, if applicable, suggesting improvements. Referees are encouraged (but not required) to add reports for articles they approve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate publication (publish then filter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles submitted to F1000 Research are first processed through an in-house sanity check and then, assuming they pass, published immediately. Post-publication they are subjected to formal peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'publish first/referee openly later' approach prioritizes speed and fairness: good science can enter the record immediately and the community can evaluate it. Strengths cited: fast dissemination, prevention of publication blocking, openness. Concerns (e.g., risk of junk) are addressed by relying on community review and visible referee reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-house sanity check before publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles are first processed through an in-house sanity check and then, assuming they pass, published immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implies a minimal pre-publication screening to filter out non-scientific or clearly inappropriate submissions while keeping substantive peer review post-publication. The piece frames this as a lightweight gate to allow immediate publication of bona fide scientific work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open refereeing: publish referee reports and name referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees’ reports are published on the site and all referees are named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openly publishing reports and naming referees increases transparency, discourages bias, and allows readers to see the back-and-forth between authors and referees. The article argues that openness does not prevent critical reviews; referees have been willing to criticize in public, and authors can respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author response and iterative versioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors have the opportunity to respond to a referee’s comments and are encouraged to update their articles and publish revised versions on the site. All versions are separately citable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages an ongoing conversation: authors can address critiques, post revisions, and maintain a transparent record of changes. Separate citation of versions preserves provenance and allows readers to follow improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear labeling of referee/review status
rubrics_metrics.description: All articles and all versions are clearly marked with their referee status and articles that have not yet been refereed are labeled as 'Awaiting Review.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit status labels help readers interpret the reliability and review progress of each article/version. This is part of transparency and reduces confusion about whether a piece has been evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary review: explain significance and put work in perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: F1000 Faculty Members write brief recommendations explaining what makes the work significant and putting the science in perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary post-publication review acts as positive filtering: short expert commentaries highlight notable papers and contextualize findings for readers who cannot keep up with the volume of literature. Recommendations should be concise, explain significance, and provide perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection by named experts (Faculty Members/Associates)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 10,000 named Faculty Members and their Associates select articles that impress them, regardless of source, and write brief recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of clearly identified experts provides context for opinions and helps readers weigh recommendations. Expertise is necessary to navigate specialized fields; naming reviewers avoids anonymous endorsements and increases accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer openness over pre-publication secrecy and gatekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: F1000 links most weaknesses of standard peer review to two core issues: that it is conducted pre-publication and that it is secret. Pre-publication peer review allows delay, filtering, and interruption; secrecy makes problems impossible to resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt post-publication, open review to reduce delays and censorship-like effects of closed pre-publication review. Openness reframes peer review as expert criticism/advice rather than behind-the-scenes gatekeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish valid science regardless of novelty or perceived 'interest'
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not need to know if it’s exciting, or novel, or ground-breaking, we simply want to know that it’s valid; ... Uninteresting science is still science, and we believe it should be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reviewers should not use novelty or perceived interest as sole grounds to block publication of valid work; the record should include sound but incremental or niche studies as well as high-profile findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community evaluation and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: F1000 Research will publish good science and let the community decide what the ultimate value of a specific piece of work is ... sloppy work will be publicly described as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on transparent, public review and community attention to surface strengths and weaknesses. Public negative reviews act as accountability and deterrent against submitting low-quality work; ultimate judgment is collective and ongoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive filtering as value-added service
rubrics_metrics.description: The F1000 article recommendation service applies a layer of positive filtering on top of traditionally peer reviewed literature; we review already-published biology and medicine in order to identify and promote the best work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive filtering (recommendations by experts) helps researchers find important papers across many journals and disciplines. It complements, rather than replaces, primary review by highlighting papers that 'impress' experts and explaining why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anonymous secondary recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that F1000’s reviewers are named puts their opinions in perspective. No one has ever suggested that our F1000 Faculty Members should conduct this form of post-publication review anonymously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For secondary recommendations, naming reviewers is considered important for credibility and context; anonymity is presented as undesirable for this model.
